title: HALLOWEEN: THE NIGHT CHRISTIANS ARE DIVIDED—AND THE QUESTION JESUS MAY BE ASKING YOU
paragraphs: HALLOWEEN: THE NIGHT CHRISTIANS ARE DIVIDED—AND THE QUESTION JESUS MAY BE ASKING YOU

Before you put on the costume, open the door to trick-or-treaters, or condemn the Christian who does, there is something Scripture says about darkness, holiness, conscience, and grace that every follower of Jesus needs to understand.
A little girl stood in front of the mirror, smiling.

Her costume was ready. Her little plastic pumpkin was waiting by the door. Outside, children were laughing, neighbors were decorating their houses, and the streets were slowly filling with people preparing for another Halloween night.
Then she turned toward her mother and asked a question that made the room go quiet.
“Mommy, does Jesus get sad when Christians celebrate Halloween?”
Her mother stopped.
Because suddenly, this wasn't about candy anymore.
It wasn't about costumes, pumpkins, or decorations.
It was about something far deeper.
How do you teach a child to love Jesus without teaching her to be afraid of everything?
How do you protect a young heart from darkness without making her believe darkness is more powerful than Christ?
And how do you explain holiness in a world where Christians themselves cannot agree on what faithfulness should look like?
Perhaps you've asked the same question.
Maybe you grew up celebrating Halloween without ever thinking twice about it.
Maybe you grew up in a Christian home where Halloween was strictly forbidden.
Maybe you are a parent trying to make the right decision, afraid that one careless choice could influence your children's spiritual lives.
Or maybe you are the Christian who secretly wonders whether the church has become so occupied with fighting over October 31 that we have forgotten how to reach the people standing outside our doors.
Whatever brought you here, please don't leave before we examine what the Bible actually says.
Because the question is not simply whether Christians should celebrate Halloween.
The deeper question is whether Jesus Christ truly has authority over the way we live—even in the ordinary choices that everyone else considers harmless.
And the answer may challenge both the Christian who celebrates Halloween and the Christian who condemns everyone who does.
There is a danger in participating without discernment.
But there is also a danger in condemning without biblical understanding.
Both can reveal a heart that needs to return to Jesus.
So what does Scripture really teach?
First, we need to establish something important.
The Bible does not specifically mention Halloween.
There is no verse that says, “Thou shalt not celebrate October 31.”
And there is no verse that commands Christians to participate in Halloween celebrations.
Anyone who claims otherwise is going beyond what Scripture explicitly says.
But the absence of the word Halloween from the Bible does not mean Christians are left without guidance.
Scripture gives us principles concerning idolatry, occult practices, holiness, conscience, Christian liberty, love for others, and the glory of God.
And those principles matter enormously.
In Deuteronomy 18:10–12, God prohibited His people from practicing divination, sorcery, witchcraft, consulting the dead, and other forms of occult activity.
The Hebrew word קֶסֶם (qesem) refers to divination—attempting to obtain hidden knowledge or guidance through forbidden spiritual means.
These prohibitions were not about innocent costumes or children receiving candy. They addressed actual practices through which people sought supernatural power or knowledge apart from God.
The distinction matters.
Because biblical faithfulness requires us to condemn what God condemns without pretending He has condemned things the passage does not address.
If a Halloween activity involves actual occult rituals, attempts to communicate with the dead, invocation of spirits, or participation in witchcraft, a Christian should refuse it.
Not because Satan is equal to God.
Not because a date on the calendar possesses supernatural authority.
But because allegiance to Jesus is incompatible with seeking spiritual power from sources He forbids.
The apostle Paul makes a similar distinction in 1 Corinthians 10.

He warns believers against participation in idolatrous worship, while also explaining that food sold in the marketplace need not automatically be rejected merely because of its possible association with pagan sacrifice.
Paul was neither careless about idolatry nor superstitious about ordinary objects.
He understood that worship, participation, knowledge, conscience, and love all matter.
And then he gave a principle that reaches far beyond his original discussion.
“So whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” — 1 Corinthians 10:31, ESV
Whatever you do.
That includes the entertainment you consume.
The celebrations you attend.
The traditions you preserve.
The things you teach your children.
And yes, even the decisions you make about Halloween.
The question becomes painfully personal.
Can I sincerely do this to the glory of God?
Not merely because everyone else is doing it.
Not because I am afraid of disappointing my friends.
Not because I want to prove that Christians are free to do whatever they want.
But because my heart genuinely desires to honor Jesus Christ.
That is where Christian discernment begins.
And that is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we want God to give us a rule when He is calling us to examine our motives.
We want someone to tell us exactly how far we can go without crossing the line.
How frightening can the costume be?
How dark can the movie become?
How much fascination with evil is acceptable before it begins shaping our affections?
But the Christian life was never intended to be a competition to see how close we can stand to darkness without falling into it.
It is a life of following the One who brought us out of darkness.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” — Ephesians 5:8, ESV
Look carefully at the language.
Paul does not merely say that believers once lived in darkness.
He says they were darkness.
And now, in the Lord, they are light.
The Greek expression τέκνα φωτός (tekna phōtos) means “children of light.”
It describes people whose identity and conduct are shaped by their relationship with God.
This is not a command to panic whenever we see a skeleton decoration.
It is a command to live consistently with the new identity Christ has given us.
A plastic skeleton does not automatically constitute occult participation.
A child dressed as a firefighter is not practicing pagan worship.
Receiving candy is not inherently a spiritual ritual.
But neither should we pretend that every Halloween activity is spiritually neutral simply because our culture considers it entertainment.
Some celebrations glorify cruelty.
Some deliberately romanticize demonic imagery.
Some encourage fascination with practices Scripture expressly forbids.
Some entertainment makes evil look attractive, powerful, or desirable.
And a Christian must be willing to say no.
Not to prove superiority.
Not to earn salvation.
But because the One who died for us is worthy of our obedience.
Yet there is another side to this conversation that many believers overlook.
A Christian can reject Halloween and still fail to walk in the light.
Imagine a father who refuses to let his children participate in Halloween because he wants to honor God.
That decision may be thoughtful, sincere, and biblically defensible.
But imagine that same father humiliating another Christian family, calling them servants of Satan because their children wore costumes and collected candy.
He believes he is defending holiness.
But what has happened to love?
What has happened to humility?
What has happened to the gentleness Scripture commands?
Romans 14 addresses disagreements among believers over disputable matters.
Paul writes:
This passage does not make sinful behavior acceptable.
It does not turn God's explicit commands into personal preferences.
Rather, it teaches believers to distinguish between clear moral prohibitions and matters in which faithful Christians may reach different conclusions.
That distinction is essential when discussing Halloween.
A Christian participating in an occult ritual is not exercising legitimate Christian freedom.
But a Christian giving candy to neighborhood children, attending a wholesome costume gathering, or using the evening to build relationships is not necessarily participating in occult worship.
We must not erase the difference.
Because when we make our personal boundaries equal to God's commandments, we risk burdening consciences with rules God never gave.
And when we use Christian freedom as an excuse to ignore holiness, we risk treating grace as permission for carelessness.
Both errors dishonor Christ.
Paul continues in Romans 14:23:
“For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.” — ESV
The immediate context concerns acting against one's conscience in a disputed matter.
The Greek expression ἐκ πίστεως (ek pisteōs) means “from faith.”
Paul's concern is not that every activity becomes holy merely because someone feels comfortable doing it.
His point is that believers must not act against their convictions before God.
If you believe participating in a particular Halloween activity would compromise your faithfulness to Christ, do not participate.
Do not violate your conscience merely to fit in.
And if you believe a particular activity is permissible, do not use that freedom to pressure another believer to act against theirs.
Christian maturity is not measured by how many freedoms you can defend.
It is measured by how faithfully you love and obey Jesus.
But perhaps you're wondering where Halloween came from in the first place.
The history is more complicated than many viral posts suggest.

Halloween developed through a mixture of historical influences, including traditions associated with the ancient Gaelic festival of Samhain, Christian observances surrounding All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day, and later European and North American customs.
The word Halloween derives from All Hallows' Eve, the evening before All Saints' Day.
Some customs have pre-Christian connections. Others developed within Christian cultural settings. Still others emerged through centuries of changing folk practices and commercial celebrations.
Historians do not agree that every modern Halloween custom can be traced directly to one ancient pagan ritual.
Therefore, claiming that every pumpkin, costume, or piece of candy is inherently an act of pagan worship goes beyond what the historical evidence establishes.
But claiming that Halloween has no historical connection whatsoever to pre-Christian customs is also misleading.
The important Christian question is not simply where a custom originated.
It is what we are doing with it now, what it communicates, what it cultivates in our hearts, and whether it conflicts with God's Word.
Consider something from the early church.
Christians lived in societies filled with pagan symbols, festivals, temples, and religious practices.
They could not withdraw from every ordinary aspect of society.
Yet they were commanded to reject idolatry.
Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 8–10 demonstrates that believers needed wisdom to distinguish between everyday cultural participation and actual religious compromise.
That wisdom is still needed today.
Because the Christian who refuses to participate in Halloween may be honoring God.
And the Christian who gives candy while sharing kindness and hospitality may also be honoring God.
But neither should assume that their outward decision automatically proves the condition of their heart.
Jesus sees deeper.
And this is where I want to speak to the parent who has been quietly struggling.
You love your children.
You want them to enjoy childhood.
You want them to have beautiful memories.
But more than anything, you want them to know Jesus.
You fear becoming too strict.
You fear becoming too permissive.
You fear making the wrong decision.
And perhaps you have spent more time worrying about Halloween than praying with your children about the meaning of holiness.
Listen carefully.
Your children's spiritual formation is far bigger than one night.
They are learning about Jesus when they watch how you respond to disagreement.
They are learning about Jesus when you admit that you do not have every answer.
They are learning about Jesus when you explain why your family chooses certain things and avoids others.
They are learning about Jesus when you refuse to mock Christians who make different decisions on matters Scripture does not explicitly settle.
They are learning about Jesus when you demonstrate that obedience is rooted in love, not panic.
And they are learning about Jesus when you show them that evil is real—but Christ is greater.
First John 4:4 declares:
“He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.” — ESV
This is not permission to experiment with darkness.
It is assurance that believers do not need to live terrified of it.
Jesus Christ is not threatened by October 31.
His resurrection did not become less powerful when someone carved a pumpkin.
His victory over sin and death is not suspended because children are wearing costumes.
And His authority does not disappear when the calendar reaches Halloween.
The risen Christ declares:
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” — Matthew 28:18, ESV
All authority.
Not partial authority.
Not authority that works only inside church buildings.
All authority.
That is why Christians should approach this subject with reverence rather than superstition.
We should take spiritual evil seriously without exaggerating its power.
We should reject what Scripture forbids without inventing additional commandments.
And we should teach our children that the greatest protection they can have is not a perfectly regulated holiday calendar.
It is a growing, genuine relationship with Jesus Christ.
Still, some readers may be thinking:
“But shouldn't Christians avoid every appearance of evil?”
The phrase is often connected to 1 Thessalonians 5:22 in the King James Version:
“Abstain from all appearance of evil.”
However, the Greek expression ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ (apo pantos eidous ponērou) is commonly understood as abstaining from every kind or form of evil.
The passage is not necessarily commanding believers to avoid everything that might look suspicious to someone else.
It commands separation from actual evil.
That difference matters.
Otherwise, nearly anything could be forbidden based solely on another person's interpretation.
Jesus Himself was criticized for eating with tax collectors and sinners.
His critics misunderstood His mission.
But Jesus did not compromise holiness by extending mercy to broken people.
He entered their world without becoming enslaved to their sin.
And perhaps this brings us to one of the most neglected questions of Halloween.
What if the evening presents an opportunity to love people?
What if the family next door has been waiting for someone to notice them?
What if the lonely child walking through your neighborhood needs more than another piece of candy?
What if the exhausted parent standing at your gate has not experienced genuine Christian kindness in years?
What if your home could become a place where people encounter warmth, generosity, and a glimpse of Christlike love?
This does not mean every Christian must participate in Halloween outreach.
Nor does it mean that giving candy is equivalent to proclaiming the Gospel.
But hospitality can create opportunities for meaningful relationships.
And relationships can create opportunities to speak of Jesus.
A Christian might choose to stay home and pray.
Another might organize a church gathering.
Another might distribute treats while welcoming neighbors.
Another might avoid the festivities entirely because of personal conviction or painful past experiences.
The question is not which family can claim the most spiritual superiority.
The question is whether our choices are governed by Scripture, faith, love, and a sincere desire to glorify Christ.
Because it is possible to refuse Halloween while harboring bitterness.
And it is possible to participate in an ordinary neighborhood activity while genuinely seeking to love others.
But it is also possible to use hospitality as an excuse to indulge entertainment that is damaging your conscience.
We must be honest enough to examine all of it.
Especially the parts that challenge our preferences.
Perhaps this article has made you uncomfortable.
Perhaps you wanted a simple yes.
Or a simple no.
Something you could screenshot, share, and use to win an argument.
But discipleship is not always about winning arguments.
Sometimes it is about allowing the Word of God to expose the motives we would rather keep hidden.
Why do you celebrate?
Why do you refuse?
Are you following conviction or merely copying your culture?
Are you defending holiness or protecting your pride?
Are you exercising freedom or resisting accountability?
Are you protecting your children or teaching them fear?
Are you reaching your neighbors or simply trying to appear more spiritual than they are?
These questions are worth asking.
Not because Halloween is the greatest spiritual issue facing the church.
But because ordinary decisions often reveal extraordinary truths about our hearts.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is this:
We could spend an entire evening arguing about darkness while neglecting the people Jesus commanded us to love.
We could condemn costumes while overlooking cruelty.
We could reject frightening decorations while secretly feeding bitterness, pornography, greed, unforgiveness, or hypocrisy.
We could pride ourselves on avoiding a controversial holiday while refusing to repent of sins that Scripture plainly identifies.
And then we could congratulate ourselves for being holy.
Jesus warned against this kind of spiritual blindness.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked religious leaders who were meticulous about certain religious obligations while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
His rebuke was not against obedience.
It was against distorted priorities and hypocrisy.
That warning should humble us.
Because holiness is not a costume we wear to convince others we belong to God.
Holiness is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
The Greek word ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos), often translated “sanctification” or “holiness,” refers to being set apart for God and the process of living in a manner consistent with that belonging.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3, Paul writes:
Holiness is not merely avoiding certain cultural activities.
It is belonging to God with our bodies, desires, decisions, relationships, and conduct.
It means rejecting genuine sin.
It means loving truth.
It means practicing repentance.
It means extending grace.
It means learning to desire what honors Christ.
And when we fail, it means returning to the Savior who is faithful to forgive.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we can make ourselves righteous by avoiding Halloween.
Not that our freedom to celebrate proves we are spiritually mature.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, we receive forgiveness and new life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” — ESV
No one may boast.
Not the Christian who celebrates.
Not the Christian who abstains.
Not the parent who has every household rule carefully arranged.
Not the believer who has never touched a Halloween decoration.
Our confidence is not in our ability to manage a holiday perfectly.
Our confidence is in Jesus Christ.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and live for Him.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.
Grace is not the enemy of holiness.
Grace is what teaches us to pursue it.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message has always been so much deeper than public appearances.
Think about that.
Some of us have stories we would never want displayed in public.
Some have practiced things Scripture condemns.
Some have lived in spiritual darkness.
Some have been deceived.
Some have judged others mercilessly while hiding their own failures.
Some have been wounded by religious people who knew how to condemn but did not know how to love.
And some are still trying to understand how a holy God could welcome someone with such a complicated past.
But the cross answers that question.
Jesus does not save people because their stories are clean.
He saves sinners by His grace.
He calls us to repentance, forgives us, and begins transforming our lives.
Your past does not have to be your future.
Your failures do not have to be your identity.
And your spiritual growth does not have to end where your understanding is today.
If you have been involved in genuine occult practices, turn away from them and seek Christ.
If you have participated in things that violated your conscience, confess them to God.
If you have condemned fellow believers without understanding Scripture, repent of that too.
If you have used Christian liberty to excuse spiritually destructive choices, bring those choices before the Lord.
And if you have been so afraid of making a mistake that your faith has become dominated by anxiety, remember the Savior who invites His people to trust Him.
Jesus does not call us to careless freedom.
He calls us to faithful freedom.
A freedom that is obedient.
A freedom that loves.
A freedom that refuses idolatry.
A freedom that does not enslave other believers to human rules.
A freedom that asks, again and again:
“Lord Jesus, how can I honor You here?”
So, should Christians participate in Halloween celebrations?
Christians must reject occult practices, idolatry, and activities that glorify genuine evil. But Scripture does not establish a universal prohibition against every modern Halloween custom.
Participation in ordinary, non-occult activities requires discernment concerning conscience, content, motives, influence, and love for others.
Some Christians will reasonably conclude that abstaining is the wisest and most faithful choice for their families.
Others may participate in carefully chosen activities without violating any clear biblical command.
Both should submit their decisions to Christ.
Neither should despise the other over matters Scripture leaves open to conscience.
And no believer should compromise a clear biblical command merely because a cultural tradition has become popular.
That is not a convenient answer.
It requires thought.
Prayer.
Humility.
Scripture.
Self-examination.
And sometimes the courage to disappoint people on either side of the debate.
But that is what following Jesus looks like.
It is not always easy.
It is not always popular.
And it cannot always be reduced to a slogan.

Tonight, when children are laughing in the streets, when families are gathering, when social media is overflowing with arguments, and when Christians are once again debating what should or should not happen on October 31, remember this:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Not just on Sunday.
Not just during worship.
Not just when we open our Bibles.
He is Lord over our entertainment, traditions, relationships, homes, convictions, and decisions.
And one day, the greatest question will not be whether we won the Halloween argument.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Him.
Whether we trusted His Gospel.
Whether we followed His Word.
Whether we loved the people He placed around us.
Whether we allowed His grace to transform the way we lived.
So before you close this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Has this discussion exposed an area where you have been careless with your faith—or perhaps too quick to judge someone else's?
You don't need to pretend that you have everything figured out.

And if God has been teaching you to balance biblical conviction with Christlike love, share what you have learned. Your testimony might encourage another believer who is wrestling with the same question.
Because our mission is not to win arguments about holidays.
Our mission is to proclaim Christ.
And that mission requires more than one article.
It requires ongoing biblical teaching, discipleship, prayerful preparation, resources, and a community willing to help carry the Gospel message farther.
Scripture teaches:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, ESV
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the idea that you must pay to prove your love for Jesus.
But a willing partnership in helping others hear His Word.
Pray for this ministry.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Open your Bible with someone who is searching for truth.
A faithful witness is not measured by the amount of money someone gives.
It is measured by faithfulness to the Lord.
Because ministries are servants.
Christ is the Savior.
And He alone deserves the glory.
Now, before you return to the noise of the world, remember the little girl standing in front of the mirror.
The one who asked whether Jesus becomes sad when Christians celebrate Halloween.
Perhaps the most important thing her mother could teach her is not merely a rule about one evening.
It is how to open the Bible.
How to recognize genuine evil.
How to obey God with a sincere conscience.
How to treat people with kindness.
How to disagree without hatred.
How to repent when she is wrong.
And how to trust Jesus more than she fears the darkness.
Because long after the costumes are put away, the decorations disappear, and the candy is forgotten, that little girl will still need a Savior.
So will her mother.
So will the Christian who celebrates.
So will the Christian who abstains.
And so will you and I.
The greatest danger is not that darkness will own one night of the year, but that we might spend our lives debating the darkness while failing to surrender our hearts to the Light.
